title: After My Clerkship at the University of North Carolina
paragraphs: I was given the opportunity to study for two months at the University of North Carolina in the United States. With gratitude to the many people who supported me, I would like to write this account of my experience.

In the first month I was on the pulmonology consult team. Every morning I was assigned one consult coming in from another department, took the patient's history and examined the patient, gave the attending a presentation including the assessment and plan, and wrote in the chart, and then we decided on the plan through the team's discussion and rounds. Because it was a small team of three, the attending, a fellow and me, my questions and opinions in discussions were listened to properly, and I was able to do my clerkship in a fortunate environment. Many of the cases were requests for a differential diagnosis from abnormal shadows on imaging and from the history, and they were all complex cases, so it was nearly impossible for me actually to make the differential diagnosis and even think of a treatment plan. However, it was very meaningful that I could train in the initial approach to reaching a diagnosis: what possibilities should be considered, what at the very least must be excluded, and which tests are needed for that, which are not needed and which must not be done. At first, after my presentation, the attending often said, "So, what's the patient's problem?" What is important is not guessing the differential, but thinking one by one about what the patient's problems are now and what should be done about them.

In the second month I was on the pediatric pulmonology inpatient team. I was puzzled that nearly 70% of the patients had cystic fibrosis, a disease that one almost never sees in Japan, but from the second week, when I had gradually gotten used to it, I was assigned two patients and followed them until discharge. Every day I took the history and did the physical examination, gave a brief presentation in SOAP format and wrote in the chart, and received feedback on it from the attending. Building a plan aiming at the goal of the patient's "discharge" was very difficult, and not only the treatment plan during hospitalization but also whether the family was ready to receive the child, home care such as tracheal tubes, and the choice of antibiotics were things I worked on every day, drawing on discussions involving many professions such as pharmacists, dietitians, nurses and care managers. At the end of the clerkship, giving a case presentation on an interesting case at a joint conference with other departments, including an introduction of recent literature, was also a very valuable experience.

During the clerkship there were several episodes in which I felt the differences between medicine in Japan and in the United States. There was the attending of the consult team who discussed a single patient for two hours, and the fellows in pediatric pulmonology, who spend most of the year on their own research and normally do ward work for only one or two months a year in rotation. I felt that this is a "relaxed" way of using time that is possible only in the United States, where work is highly specialized and subdivided. Facing a patient with severe interstitial pneumonia, the doctor said just one thing: "This patient has nothing left but a lung transplant." I imagined that in Japan today there might not even be the option of "lung transplant" (though I do not know about the future...). On the other hand, there are also patients who, even with early-stage lung cancer for which surgery is indicated, have no insurance and so can only be followed in the outpatient clinic without any treatment. Actually "experiencing" American medicine in this way led me to look again at both the strengths and weaknesses of Japanese medicine.

The experience of plunging, while still a student, into a different culture and a different healthcare system greatly broadened my own horizons and was the best opportunity to think about my future. The female attending who took very good care of me gave me a message at the end: "Don't be a stranger." It felt like words that exactly expressed what had been in my heart throughout my stay in the United States, although I had not been conscious of it. She went on to say that I will surely become a wonderful doctor, so I should come back to the United States again with confidence, and that she would certainly help me when I do. I was truly happy, and it was a moment when I thought it had been right to study abroad. If any junior student is interested in this study abroad program but hesitating, I would like to give them the same words and tell them to take up the challenge with confidence. I am sure you will gain an irreplaceable asset.

Outside the clerkship too, I have only very happy memories, such as joining a local choir and traveling around the United States with friends on weekends. Every day I deeply felt how grateful I was that there were people who helped me sincerely in an unfamiliar environment, starting with my host family, who took very good care of me. I sincerely thank the professors of the International Exchange Office, the people in the Academic Affairs office, the professors and seniors who guided us in the pre-departure training, and all my classmates, starting with 小松, who worked hard together with me at UNC, for giving me this valuable opportunity. Thank you very much.
